Stablecoin sandwich: how it works, what it costs

By the Ibanora teamPublished November 25, 20268 min read

In short

A stablecoin sandwich is a cross-border payment that turns one currency into a stablecoin, moves the stablecoin over a blockchain, and turns it into another currency at the other end. An October 2026 IMF working paper found that most of the cost sits at the two ends, in trading fees and fiat deposit and withdrawal fees, while blockchain transfer fees made up less than a quarter of it.

A stablecoin sandwich is a way to send money abroad in three layers: ordinary money goes in, a dollar stablecoin carries the value across the border, and ordinary money comes out. The IMF working paper Deconstructing the Stablecoin Sandwich, published on October 30, 2026, sums it up as "fiat in, stablecoin transfer, fiat out."

The case for using stablecoins in cross-border payments often rests on the low cost of the blockchain transfer itself, the IMF authors note. They measured the whole chain instead, across 270 directed corridors between 18 sample countries, with 29 exchanges and 4,005 complete routes, and found most of the cost in the fiat and exchange steps at either end.

What is a stablecoin sandwich?

The IMF paper defines it as a retail transfer in which fiat money buys a US dollar stablecoin in the sending country, the stablecoin moves on-chain between exchanges, and it is then sold for local currency and withdrawn to a bank account in the receiving country. The authors call this the dominant structure for exchange-based stablecoin cross-border payments.

Banks, payment service providers and local payment methods still move the money where it enters and leaves, so, in the IMF's words, stablecoins "do not eliminate the role of traditional payment infrastructure." For the tokens themselves, see what a stablecoin is.

How a fiat to stablecoin to fiat transfer works

The IMF paper follows a transfer through five stages:

  1. Fiat deposit: the sender pays money into an exchange, for example by bank transfer or card.
  2. Stablecoin purchase: the exchange sells stablecoins at its local price and takes a trading fee.
  3. On-chain transfer: the stablecoins move to the second exchange over a network such as Ethereum or Tron.
  4. Stablecoin sale: the recipient's exchange buys them for local currency and takes a trading fee.
  5. Fiat withdrawal: the recipient withdraws the local currency to a bank account.

In the paper's stylized example, which uses assumed fees, a sender puts in 200 units of a currency, with fiat fees of 0.25% at each end, trading fees of 0.40% on each leg, a flat stablecoin withdrawal fee of 0.5, and local stablecoin prices 0.80% above the benchmark exchange rate at the origin and 0.30% above it at the destination. The losses, valued in the sender's currency:

StageWhat is chargedLost (of 200)
Fiat deposit0.25% deposit fee0.50
Stablecoin purchaseOrigin premium, spread and trading fee2.57
On-chain transferFlat withdrawal fee of 0.5 stablecoin0.50
Stablecoin saleSpread and trading fee, partly offset by the destination premium0.39
Fiat withdrawal0.25% plus a flat fee of 2 units of the destination currency0.99
TotalCost of the transfer4.95 (2.47%)

Source: IMF WP/26/230, Table A2.

Where the costs sit in a stablecoin sandwich

With real fees, the IMF estimates the average cost of a $200 transfer at 2.18% across its 270 corridors, with a median of 1.99% and a range of -2.18% to 8.03%. The fees come from exchanges' public pages at the start of the second quarter of 2026, assuming users pick the cheapest fiat method, usually a standard bank transfer. The average splits into four groups:

Cost groupAverage share of a $200 transferWhat it covers
Trading fees0.85%Exchange fees for buying and selling the stablecoin, both legs
Fiat rail fees0.67%Fiat deposit and withdrawal fees at the two exchanges
Crypto transfer0.48%Stablecoin withdrawal and deposit fees for the on-chain leg
Premium and spread0.18%, ranging from -3.07% to 4.51%Gap between local stablecoin prices and the benchmark exchange rate, plus the bid-ask spread

Source: IMF WP/26/230, Table 4. Blockchain transfer fees made up less than a quarter of the average cost. The authors place the main costs in domestic exchange infrastructure, stablecoin pricing and access to fiat payment rails. They warn that judging stablecoin payments on blockchain fees alone risks overstating the cost advantage.

On the destination side, fiat withdrawal fees averaged 0.37% and trading fees 0.41%. Where only a few banks, payment providers or local exchanges serve stablecoin users, the paper adds, transfers can become sensitive to those banking relationships, the local payment system and the fiat liquidity available in that currency.

Why the same corridor can cost more one way

The IMF paper treats the premium like the exchange-rate margin on a traditional remittance. An origin premium leaves the sender with fewer stablecoins, and a destination premium gives the recipient more local currency.

In the sample, Korean stablecoin prices tended to sit above the benchmark, making Korea expensive to send from and cheap to receive into. Where the destination premium is large enough, the measured cost turns negative. The paper says this "does not imply that users are paid to remit." It reflects a pricing distortion, which can come from market segmentation, strong local demand for dollar assets or limits to arbitrage. The Korean premium narrowed and even reversed in the first half of 2026, the authors add.

Is a stablecoin sandwich cheaper than a bank transfer or remittance?

Sometimes. The IMF paper measures against the G20 target of 3% for the cost of a remittance. The Financial Stability Board (FSB) includes a remittance cost target, dated 2030, among its targets for cross-border payments on cost, speed, transparency and access. The IMF paper cites World Bank data putting the global average cost of sending $200 at 6.36% in the third quarter of 2025.

The IMF's 2.18% average is below the target. In the 33 corridors with traditional price data, the average stablecoin cost was almost 5 percentage points below the traditional average. But comparing the cheapest stablecoin route with the cheapest traditional provider in each corridor, the traditional option was still cheaper in about one third of them.

Two choices move the result a lot:

  • Transfer size. The mean cost fell from 4.12% at $50 to 1.54% at $5,000, because some fees are flat amounts.
  • The fiat method. Median-cost or most expensive deposit and withdrawal methods raised the mean to 3.04% and 4.07%. The costlier methods were also faster, the authors note, though they could not check this for every corridor.

The estimates leave out speed, search and onboarding effort, counterparty risk, and the compliance costs that intermediaries carry.

Two compliance checks, one at each end

In the IMF's model, each end of the sandwich is an exchange that onboards its own customer. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) says many users reach stablecoins through hosted wallets at crypto exchanges whose onboarding in principle should be similar to a bank's, and that many jurisdictions hold exchanges and wallet providers to standards similar to banks.

The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) applies its anti-money laundering standards to virtual asset service providers through Recommendation 15. In its June 2025 update, it said 99 jurisdictions had passed or were passing laws for the Travel Rule, which it describes as ensuring transparency of information around cross-border payments. In the EU, the Transfer of Funds Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 has applied since December 30, 2024. Under Article 14, the sender's crypto-asset service provider must make sure the transfer carries the names of the originator and the beneficiary, their blockchain addresses, and identifying details about the originator.

Issuers run their own check: the IMF paper says they mint and redeem only with approved counterparties that have passed the issuer's compliance process, so most users trade on exchanges. The IMF did not measure compliance costs, but its conclusion suggests that capital flow regimes, AML/CFT requirements and exchange licensing regimes, among other factors, play an important role in explaining differences in transfer costs.

Stablecoin settlement: what the blockchain leg does

The IMF paper calls blockchain networks the settlement and record-keeping layer for the stablecoin. Two points follow:

  • Both exchanges must support the same stablecoin on the same network, so there can be far fewer workable routes than exchanges.
  • If both users hold accounts at the same platform, the transfer can be an entry on its internal ledger, with no blockchain transaction.

The BIS contrasts this with bank payments, which settle finally on the central bank's accounts. Stablecoins lack that function, it says, and each carries its issuer's name, so different stablecoins can trade at different rates.

Full vs open sandwich

As of November 2026, a guide from Polygon describes a full sandwich as fiat in, stablecoin across and fiat out, with neither sender nor recipient handling stablecoins. In an open, or half, sandwich, the recipient keeps the stablecoins and converts them to fiat later, or not at all.

The IMF figures cover only transfers in which the recipient sells the stablecoin for local currency on an exchange and withdraws it to a bank account. They leave out cases where the recipient holds the stablecoin, peer-to-peer transfers and decentralized exchanges. In an open sandwich the recipient holds a token, so its terms matter. In the EU, MiCA gives holders of an e-money token a claim against its issuer. Article 49 says the issuer must redeem it at any time and at par value, and that redemption is not subject to a fee, except for measures the issuer's recovery plan allows under Article 46.

How regulators approach stablecoins in cross-border payments

In July 2023 the FSB finalized its high-level recommendations for global stablecoin arrangements. They aim for consistent and effective regulation, supervision and oversight across jurisdictions, to address potential financial stability risks.

MiCA (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114) applies from December 30, 2024, and its titles on asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens from June 30, 2024. Under Article 48, only an issuer authorized as a credit institution or electronic money institution may offer an e-money token to the public in the EU, though others may do so with the issuer's written consent. Under Article 59, only an authorized crypto-asset service provider, or one of the financial firms allowed under Article 60, may provide crypto-asset services in the EU.

The FATF's March 2026 report on stablecoins and unhosted wallets points to peer-to-peer transfers without any regulated intermediary. It says only a limited number of jurisdictions have rules aimed at stablecoins. Its good practices include requiring issuers to be able to freeze or burn tokens and to carry out customer due diligence at redemption.

What to check before you use one

  • What the recipient gets in their currency, against what you send at the benchmark exchange rate.
  • Deposit and withdrawal fees at each end, the payment method assumed, and any flat fees, which weigh more on small transfers.
  • Who pays out in the recipient's country, and to which bank accounts.
  • For an open sandwich, which stablecoin the recipient will hold, who issued it and its redemption rights.

Questions

Why don't banks like stablecoins?

One official answer comes from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). It argues that stablecoins fall short of three tests for the core of a monetary system: singleness, elasticity and integrity. It says each stablecoin carries its issuer's name and can trade at its own rate, that new tokens need full payment upfront, and that stablecoins held in unhosted wallets escape know-your-customer checks.

Which stablecoins does the IMF study?

The IMF paper of October 2026 studies USDT, issued by Tether, and USDC, issued by Circle. Our guide to what a stablecoin is lists more examples.

How do stablecoin issuers make money?

According to the IMF paper of October 2026, the largest issuers earn most of their revenue from interest on reserve assets, mainly US Treasury securities, rather than from transaction fees. The paper adds that issuers sometimes share this reserve income with distribution partners, which can lead exchanges to charge different trading fees on different stablecoins.

Do stablecoins pay interest in the EU?

Not on e-money tokens. Under MiCA Article 50, issuers of e-money tokens may not grant interest, and crypto-asset service providers may not grant interest on services related to e-money tokens. Any benefit tied to how long someone holds the token counts as interest.
